content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a global report in 2014 highlighting drowning as a leading cause of death and emphasizing the need for prevention strategies. 2. WHO released guidelines in 2004 for conducting community surveys on injuries and violence to better understand and address these issues. 3. Mello-Jorge and Marques, in 1985, analyzed violent childhood deaths in Brazil, providing critical insights into the epidemiology of such fatalities. 4. Rahman et al. (2012) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of an injury and drowning prevention program in Bangladesh, demonstrating its potential impact on reducing childhood mortality. 5. Thompson et al. (2000) reviewed the effectiveness of pool fencing in preventing drowning among children, as documented in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 6. Depczynski et al. (2009) explored the role of safe play areas in preventing young children from drowning in farm dams, as published in the Australasian Journal of Early Childhood. 7. Iqbal et al. (2007) investigated childhood mortality due to drowning in rural Matlab, Bangladesh, and proposed solutions to mitigate the problem. 8. Hyder et al. (2014) developed a framework to address the implementation gap in global drowning prevention interventions, drawing from experiences in Bangladesh. 9. Hyder et al. also documented the Saving of Children’s Lives from Drowning project in Bangladesh, published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 10. Callaghan et al. (2010) conducted a pilot study on child supervision practices for drowning prevention in rural Bangladesh, utilizing innovative supervision tools. 11. Islam et al. (2015) presented preliminary findings on the use of playpens to prevent child drowning in rural Bangladesh at the World Conference on Drowning Prevention. 12. Bennett and Linnan (2014) discussed the role of physical barriers in drowning prevention in the book Drowning: Prevention, Rescue, Treatment. 13. Yeh et al. (2011) analyzed injuries associated with cribs, playpens, and bassinets among young children in the U.S. from 1990 to 2008, as published in Pediatrics. 14. Cordovil et al. (2009) examined the efficacy of safety barriers for children, including their absolute effectiveness and the time required to cross them, in the International Journal of Injury Control and Safety Promotion. 15. The Federal Register (2010) outlined safety standards for full-size and non-full-size baby cribs, emphasizing third-party testing for certain children’s products. 16. Nixon et al. (1979) conducted an ergonomic study on childproof safety barriers to reduce trauma from environmental hazards, published in the Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health. 17. Guevarra et al. (2015) initiated discussions on child drowning prevention in the Philippines, as documented in the International Journal of Injury Control and Safety Promotion. 18. Celis (1997) analyzed home drowning incidents among preschool-aged Mexican children, published in Injury Prevention. 19. Ellis and Trent (1997) studied swimming pool drownings and near-drownings among California preschoolers, as reported in Public Health Reports. 20. Pearn et al. (2008) reviewed the impact of safety legislation and public health policy on drowning prevention in the International Journal of Injury Control and Safety Promotion. 21. Stevenson et al. (2003) examined barriers surrounding private swimming pools to prevent childhood drowning, as published in Pediatrics. 22. WHO’s 2008 report on child injury prevention provided a comprehensive overview of strategies to reduce injuries globally. 23. WHO’s 2014 fact sheet on drowning highlighted the global burden of drowning and the need for targeted interventions. 24. Linnan et al. (2012) presented evidence on child drowning as a significant cause of mortality in lowand middle-income countries, emphasizing prevention strategies. 25. Linnan et al. (2007) provided an overview of child mortality and injury in Asia, published by UNICEF Innocenti Research Centre. 26. Stallman et al. (2014) discussed swimming and water survival competence in the book Drowning: Prevention, Rescue, Treatment. 27. Brenner et al. (2009) conducted a case-control study on the association between swimming lessons and childhood drowning, published in the Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine. 28. Yang et al. (2007) identified risk factors for childhood drowning in rural regions of a developing country, as published in Injury Prevention. 29. Rahman et al. (2005) reported on the Bangladesh Health and Injury Survey, focusing on child injury prevention. 30. Rahman et al. (2012) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of injury and drowning prevention programs in Bangladesh, as published in Pediatrics. 31. Mecrow et al. (2015) investigated whether teaching children to swim increases exposure or risk-taking in water, with evidence from Bangladesh. 32. Mecrow et al. also described children rescuing other children from drowning in rural Bangladesh, as published in Injury Prevention. 33. The United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015) emphasized sustainable development and disaster risk management in its global assessment report. 34. Jonkman and Kelman (2005) analyzed the causes and circumstances of flood disaster deaths, as published in Disasters. 35. Haynes et al. (2009) compared shelter-in-place versus evacuation strategies during flash floods, as documented in Environmental Hazards. 36. Jonkman (2014) provided a general overview of flood-related mortality in the book Drowning: Prevention, Rescue, Treatment. 37. Diakakis and Deligiannakis (2015) studied flood fatalities in Greece from 1970 to 2010, as published in the Journal of Flood Risk Management. 38. Jonkman et al. (2009) analyzed mortality caused by flooding in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, published in Risk Analysis. 39. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2014) synthesized findings on climate change impacts, adaptation, and vulnerability. 40. Hirabayashi et al. (2013) assessed global flood risk under climate change, as published in Nature Climate Change. 41. Hallegatte et al. (2013) projected future flood losses in major coastal cities, as documented in Nature Climate Change. 42. Chan et al. (2012) examined flood risk in Asia’s urban mega-deltas, focusing on drivers, impacts, and responses, as published in Environmental and Urbanization Asia. 43. Syvitski et al. (2009) analyzed the sinking of deltas due to human activities, as published in Nature Geoscience. 44. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030) outlined global strategies for disaster risk reduction. 45. Daellenbach et al. (2015) emphasized community response planning in disaster management, as documented by Victoria University of Wellington. 46. Benson et al. (2016) evaluated social learning in flood risk management in England, as published in Environmental Science & Policy. 47. Van Den Honert and McAneney (2011) analyzed the causes, impacts, and implications of the 2011 Brisbane floods, as published in Water. 48. The Australian Attorney-General’s Department (2013) provided a guide to best practices in flood risk management. 49. Janssen et al. (2015) discussed interactive knowledge arrangements for greening flood protection, as published in the Journal of Environmental Policy & Planning. 50. Temmerman et al. (2013) highlighted ecosystem-based coastal defense in the face of global change, as published in Nature. 51. Barbier (2015) valued the storm protection services of estuarine and coastal ecosystems, as published in Ecosystem Services. 52. Jones et al. (2012) explored how nature can help people adapt to climate change, as published in Nature Climate Change. 53. Dixon et al. (2016) studied the effects of river restoration on flood risk and hydrology, as published in Earth Surface Processes and Landforms. 54. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2012) released a special report on managing risks of extreme events and disasters to advance climate change adaptation. 55. Hossain et al. (2015) identified socio-demographic, environmental, and caregiving risk factors for childhood drowning deaths in Bangladesh, as published in BMC Pediatrics. 56. Venema et al. (2010) examined the role of bystanders during the rescue and resuscitation of drowning victims, as published in Resuscitation. 57. Franklin and Pearn (2011) described the Aquatic-Victim-Instead-of-Rescuer (AVIR) syndrome, highlighting drowning fatalities involving rescuers, as published in the Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health. 58. Rahman et al. (2014) assessed the feasibility of a first responder program in rural Bangladesh, as published in Resuscitation. 59. Tate and Quan (2014) discussed cultural aspects of rescue and resuscitation of drowning victims in the book Drowning: Prevention, Rescue, Treatment. 60. Mecrow and Suvanprakorn (2014) emphasized water safety skills and knowledge in low-resource environments, as published in Drowning: Prevention, Rescue, Treatment. 61. Mecrow et al. (2015) explored the willingness to administer mouth-to-mouth ventilation in a first response program in rural Bangladesh, as published in BMC International Health and Human Rights. 62. Husum et al. (2010) described the village university experience in training pre-hospital trauma care in low-income countries, as published in Medical Teacher. 63. López-Herce et al. (2011) emphasized the importance of stable resuscitation training programs in developing countries, as published in Resuscitation. 64. The American Heart Association (2016) updated its guidelines for cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency cardiovascular care. 65. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (2016) released first aid and resuscitation guidelines. 66. The International Maritime Organization (2016) provided a list of conventions related to maritime safety. 67. Welch (2016) proposed a small-scale vessel registration system for Pacific Island countries and territories.
